clue.text: Secretary sends out returns for game, perhaps

parts.note: PA, a personal assistant, is a secretary

indicators.note: returns tells us the word for sends out comes back to front

parts.note: to emit is to send out

explanation.surface: An office secretary sends back the results of what might be a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A game is one example of a hobby or leisure activity, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Bucket covers hole at a game

indicators.note: covers says the word for bucket wraps round another piece

parts.note: to bucket down and to pelt down both mean to rain heavily
O is round like a hole

explanation.surface: A bucket is placed over a hole during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bucket' is a verb here: it buckets down, it pelts down. 'At' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Basque ball sport played against a wall with a basket strapped to the wrist.

clue.text: Small child loves snowmobile

parts.note: a kid is a child
love is zero in tennis, written O, so loves are two Os

explanation.surface: A little child adores a ride on a snowmobile.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a trade name, now generic, for a motorised sledge on skis, a snowmobile.

clue.text: Lacking a name, Indian accent needs saving

indicators.note: lacking says the following letters are missing from the word Indian

parts.note: stress is the accent, or emphasis, on a syllable

explanation.surface: An anonymous Indian voice is in need of rescue.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone or something in danger or trouble needs saving; the phrase is used of ships needing rescue.

clue.text: Hungry type at sea drinks last of rum

indicators.note: drinks says the muddled letters take in another letter
at sea means confused, so the letters of type are muddled
last of says take only the final letter of rum

explanation.surface: A ravenous sailor at sea downs the dregs of the rum.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling empty, with nothing in the stomach, means being hungry.

clue.text: Drink in a large can initially works

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: initially says take only the opening letter of the word can

parts.note: an OP (opus) is a musical work, so two of them, OP OP, are works

explanation.surface: A drink comes in a big can, and it does the trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' is plural, so it supplies two OPs, the abbreviation for opus, a numbered composition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet, fizzy, ready-mixed alcoholic beverage sold in bottles or cans, so a kind of drink.

clue.text: Actor is bamboozled by civil service word games

indicators.note: by says the next piece sits beside the jumble
bamboozled means baffled or confused, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A performer is baffled by puzzles set by civil servants.
explanation.definitionFit: Puzzles in which the first letters of lines spell a word are classic word games.

clue.text: Maybe a king or a queen breaks a record

definitions.note: a king is one example of a playing card, hence maybe

indicators.note: breaks says the record is split open to let other letters in

parts.note: CD, compact disc, is a record
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A monarch or his consort breaks a world record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King or a queen' looks like a royal pair, but only 'Maybe a king' is the definition; 'a queen' gives A and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A king is one of the court cards in a deck, so an example of a playing card.

clue.text: Refuse to be kept here training with racket, holding a pound

definitions.note: refuse is rubbish, kept in a household container until collection

indicators.note: with says the pieces join side by side

parts.note: PE is physical education, training

indicators.note: holding says the word for racket contains other letters

parts.note: a din is a loud racket
LB is the abbreviation for a pound weight

explanation.surface: Tennis training with a racket while gripping a pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb, but it is the noun rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen rubbish container with a lid opened by a foot lever is where refuse waits.

clue.text: Game bloke, one wearing ridiculous pants

indicators.note: wearing says the man and one are inside, clothed by the other piece
ridiculous suggests the letters of pants are jumbled absurdly

parts.note: he is a man, a bloke
a means one

explanation.surface: A sporty fellow in silly trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game bloke' reads as a plucky man, but 'Game' alone is the definition. In British English, pants are underpants.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-tailed bird is the most commonly shot game bird in Britain.

clue.text: Landowner's hidey-hole for game at Land's End

parts.note: a lair is the den where a wild animal, such as game, hides

indicators.note: End signals that only the final letter of Land's is wanted

explanation.surface: A landowner keeps a hiding place for wildlife out at Land's End in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Land's End is the westernmost tip of Cornwall, so the place name camouflages the last-letter instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland, the owner of a large estate is called by this title, so it is a landowner.

clue.text: Split journey, taking in golf game

parts.note: to split is to part or separate

indicators.note: taking in says one piece is placed inside the word for journey

parts.note: a ride is a journey
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A trip broken up to fit in a round of golf.
explanation.definitionFit: This plump bird is shot as game in the British countryside.

clue.text: Radical broadcaster is impressed by England batsman

indicators.note: impressed by says these pieces are pressed into the batsman's surname

parts.note: Jonathan Trott batted for England in Test cricket
Sky is a British satellite broadcaster

explanation.surface: A firebrand TV company is wowed by an England cricketer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressed' looks like admiration, but it means pressed into. Jonathan Trott was an England Test batsman around 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Leon Trotsky's revolutionary Marxism holds extreme left-wing views, so is a radical.

clue.text: It's not all child's play going over them!

definitions.text: It's not all child's play going over them!

indicators.note: going over says that run of letters is read backwards
not all says only part of the phrase child's play is used, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: Crossing a great mountain range is hard work, not child's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters S PLA sit inside 'child's play'; read backwards they give the answer, and the whole clue describes crossing these mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossing Europe's great mountain range is no easy matter, as Hannibal found.

clue.text: Polish runner-up at dice game

parts.note: to rub is to polish

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, says the word for runner is read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: a ski is a runner on snow
to dice is to cut into cubes, to cube

explanation.surface: A second-placed player brushes up on their dice game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' could be the nationality, but it is the verb rub; 'runner-up' splits into runner and up.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1970s colour-matching cube puzzle is a game, or at least a toy.

clue.text: Game Italian's behind French driver, twisting in and out

indicators.note: is behind means this piece follows the driver's name

parts.note: Alain Prost is a French Formula One world champion
IT is a short form for Italian, as in vermouth and gin

indicators.note: twisting says the letters of in and out are rearranged

explanation.surface: An Italian racer trails a French rival, weaving in and out of traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The game' is slang for prostitution. 'Twisting' rearranges IN and OUT into UTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'on the game' is British slang for working as a prostitute, so game is this trade.

clue.text: Spar commercial interrupts play on TV

indicators.note: on, in a down clue, puts one piece below another
interrupts says the commercial breaks into the word for play

parts.note: a show is a play
an ad is a commercial
the box is slang for television

explanation.surface: A television advert breaks into a broadcast drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The box' is British slang for the television.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to practise boxing, as does throwing punches at an imaginary opponent.

clue.text: It helps 8 to get out to get hog roasted

definitions.note: 8 down is a game bird; its chick uses a small hard point on the beak to crack the shell

indicators.note: roasted suggests the letters of to get hog are cooked into a new order

explanation.surface: Something that helps the game bird escape the spit while a hog is roasted.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatching chick has a hard bump on its beak for breaking the shell, so it helps the bird out.

clue.text: Glitterati check butts over

indicators.note: over says the words for check and butts are turned round

parts.note: to test is to check
rams butt with their heads, so rams are butts

explanation.surface: Fashionable celebrities check that everything is over.
explanation.definitionFit: The fashionable, sophisticated crowd of high society are the glitterati.

clue.text: Potter's art master's boring wonky Ming shapes

definitions.note: Stephen Potter wrote a humorous book on the art of winning by unsporting ploys

indicators.note: boring says one piece drills into the middle of the other
wonky says the letters of Ming shapes are skewed into a new order

parts.note: MA is the Master of Arts degree, a master's

explanation.surface: A potter's craft: the master drills into lopsided Ming vases.
explanation.walkthrough: Potter is Stephen Potter, not a ceramicist, despite the Ming vases. MA bores into GAMES NSHIP, the rearranged letters of 'Ming shapes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Potter's 1947 book popularised winning games by psychological ploys without actually cheating, his art.

clue.text: Cast rug mostly over player's back

indicators.note: over says the shortened wig goes round another letter
mostly says the slang wig loses its final letter

parts.note: rug is slang for a toupee, a wig

indicators.note: back says take the final letter of player

explanation.surface: An actor's wig, mostly, slipped down over his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rug' is slang for a hairpiece, not a carpet.
explanation.definitionFit: A company of actors is a cast, so a theatrical troupe.

clue.text: Game controller's about to take a quick look up

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, says the pieces read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: re means about, concerning
a peek is a quick look

explanation.surface: A gamer's console is about to get a quick once-over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game controller' suggests a console joypad, but it is a gamekeeper who controls game birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamekeeper manages game on an estate, a controller of game.

clue.text: Crack shot ultimately remains in it

indicators.note: ultimately says take the final letter of shot

parts.note: an urn is a vessel holding the ashes, or remains, of the dead

explanation.surface: A crack marksman's last shot, and his ashes end up in an urn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack shot' looks like one phrase, but 'Crack' alone is the definition, meaning a go.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a crack at something is to have a go, and a go is a turn.

clue.text: Continue wasting spare euros to binge

parts.note: to go on is to continue

indicators.note: wasting suggests the letters of spare plus the euro sign are squandered into a new order

parts.note: E stands for the euro, the currency

explanation.surface: Keep frittering away spare cash on a binge.
explanation.definitionFit: A spree is a bout of indulgence, so to embark on one is to binge.

clue.text: Drain out the pits

indicators.note: out means not right, so the letters of drain are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Pumping water from the mine pits.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point of anything, the absolute worst, is colloquially the pits.

clue.text: Guy reported supporters on course

definitions.note: small pegs supporting golf balls on a golf course

indicators.note: reported says the word is as said in speech

parts.note: to guy is to tease or mock

explanation.surface: A man said to have backers at the racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers rest the ball on small pegs to drive off, so these support it on the course.

clue.text: Main food grown here by Dorset moved over close to Poole

definitions.note: the main is the sea, and shellfish are farmed on this stretch of seabed

indicators.note: over says the rearranged letters cover the final letter
moved says the letters of by Dorset are shifted into a new order
close to says take the last letter of Poole

explanation.surface: Something relocated from Dorset towards the town of Poole.
explanation.walkthrough: Poole is a harbour town in Dorset, England. 'Moved' rearranges 'by Dorset' to OYSTERBD, which goes over E, the close of Poole. 'Main' is the old word for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellfish are raised on a patch of seabed set aside for them, food from the main.

clue.text: Oust no-frills insurers in recession? Yes

indicators.note: no-frills says the outer letters of the word oust are stripped off
in recession says the word for insurers goes backwards

parts.note: the Pru is the familiar name for the Prudential insurance company

explanation.surface: Should we get rid of basic insurers when the economy shrinks? Yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oust' does double duty: it is the definition, and stripped of its edges it gives US. The closing 'Yes' confirms the answer does mean oust. The Prudential is a British insurer.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize power by pushing out the holder is to oust them, a synonym.

clue.text: This ground includes a 9 to clear the field

indicators.note: includes says the rearranged word holds a letter inside it
ground means crushed up, so the letters of This are rearranged

parts.note: IX is 9 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: This cricket ground counts nine ways to send the ball over the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: '9' looks like a reference to 9 across, but it is just the Roman numeral IX. In cricket, a ball struck over the boundary without bouncing scores six runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer striking the ball clean over the boundary rope sends it right out of the field of play.

clue.text: Game rights over old English river

indicators.note: over says the two letters for rights cover the other pieces

parts.note: R is short for right, so two of them are rights
the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland

explanation.surface: A game's legal rights cover an old English river.
explanation.definitionFit: This small European deer is hunted, so counts as game.
